c.tagline: China's medieval maritime Silk Road emporium of temples, mosques, and arcade streets.

taxi.fareNote: Metered from about ¥10; most locals book via Didi and pay by Alipay/WeChat QR, so carry cash or set up mobile pay — some drivers cannot take foreign cards or make change for large notes.

emergency.note: 119 for fire; English-speaking operators are limited, so hotel staff can help translate.

hood_landmark.Xunpu Village: Xunpu Village oyster shell houses, Quanzhou

hood_desc: The living heart of the UNESCO old city (Licheng), a 1,300-year-old street of temples, snack stalls, and lantern-lit lanes anchored by the twin-pagoda Kaiyuan Temple; the best base for first-time visitors.

A restored heritage street around the 1009 Qingjing (Ashab) Mosque — the oldest Arab-style mosque in China — and the Guandi Temple, mixing Song-era stone architecture with tea houses and Minnan snacks.
China's longest continuous arcade (qilou) shopping street, a colonnaded stretch of shops, old pharmacies, and street food running straight through the old town.
Quanzhou's modern downtown around Fengze Square and Puxi Wanda Plaza, home to the city's newest malls, business hotels, and nightlife; convenient but far less historic than the old city.

A fishing village at the mouth of the Jinjiang River famous for its oyster-shell houses and the 'Zan Hua' flower-crown headdresses worn by Xunpu women; a photogenic half-day escape about 10 km from the old town.

water.note: Drink bottled or boiled water, as everywhere in mainland China.

transit.pay: Pay buses and the BRT with a local transit card, a QR code via Alipay/WeChat, or a contactless bank card; single rides run about ¥1-¥2. Foreign visitors can link an international card to Alipay or WeChat to pay by QR.
transit.hours: The BRT and main bus lines run roughly 6:00 AM to 10:30 PM, with taxis and Didi filling the late-night gap.
transit.note: Quanzhou has no metro; getting around relies on an elevated BRT busway, an extensive city bus network, taxis, and Didi ride-hailing.

landmarks: Kaiyuan Temple
Fujian's grandest Buddhist temple, founded in 686, where twin five-storey stone pagodas have towered over banyan courtyards for eight centuries.
West Street (Xi Jie)
Quanzhou's thousand-year-old main artery, a lively strip of red-brick shophouses, teahouses and snack stalls framing views of the Kaiyuan pagodas.
Qingjing Mosque
China's oldest surviving Arab-style mosque, built in 1009 by Arab merchants, its granite gate a UNESCO-listed relic of the maritime Silk Road.
Tianhou Temple
A magnificent 1196 temple to the sea goddess Mazu, the mother shrine from which her seafaring cult spread across Asia.
Luoyang Bridge
A pioneering Song-dynasty stone bay bridge of 1059, over a kilometre long, whose oyster-reinforced foundations revolutionised Chinese engineering.
Qingyuan Mountain and Laojun Rock
A sacred mountain park above the city crowned by China's largest ancient statue of Laozi, serenely carved from a single Song-dynasty boulder.
Quanzhou Maritime Museum
A museum charting the medieval port of Zayton, once the world's greatest harbour, through shipwrecks, tombstones and multi-faith relics.
Guandi Temple
An incense-wreathed temple to the god of war and wealth on Tumen Street, among the busiest and most atmospheric shrines in southern Fujian.
Chongwu Ancient Town
A remarkably complete Ming-dynasty stone garrison town by the sea, ringed by granite walls and home to the distinctive Hui'an women.
Anping Bridge
A two-kilometre Song-dynasty stone causeway across tidal flats at Anhai, long celebrated as the longest ancient bridge in China.

train.note: Quanzhou has no international trains. Quanzhou Station, about 12 km northwest of the city, is served by frequent high-speed trains on the Fujian coastal line between Fuzhou and Xiamen, with the line continuing north towards Shanghai and south towards Shenzhen and inland connections to Nanchang and Wuhan. Xiamen is well under an hour away and Fuzhou around an hour, making Quanzhou an easy stop between the two. Book on 12306 with your passport and allow half an hour to get from the station into the old town.

bus.note: No international coaches run from Quanzhou. Two main bus stations plus a smaller one near the Overseas Chinese Hotel serve Xiamen (¥27-35, about 1.5 hours) and Fuzhou (¥46-65, about 2.5 hours), with overnight services to Shenzhen, Zhuhai and Hong Kong in the ¥300 range. Tickets are sold at the counter with ID. The Hong Kong coaches are a genuine cross-boundary service requiring a passport and any needed permit, but the high-speed train covers the same ground faster.

intl.to: Kinmen/Quemoy (Taiwan) - sails from Shijing (Shuitou) passenger terminal, about 50 km south of Quanzhou, to Shuitou Pier
intl.op: Quanzhou-Kinmen ferry route — counter sales at the terminal, no online booking

ferry.note: The Kinmen boat does not leave from Quanzhou itself but from the port of Shijing roughly 50 km to the south, reached by local bus or taxi, and the crossing to Shuitou Pier on Kinmen takes about an hour for around ¥150 (NT$750). Crucially this particular route has long been restricted to mainland Chinese and Taiwanese passport holders - foreign travellers wanting to reach Kinmen should use the more frequent Wutong terminal service from neighbouring Xiamen, which runs every 30 minutes from 08:00 to 17:30 and is open to all nationalities. Either way the crossing counts as leaving mainland China, so a single-entry Chinese visa will not get you back. Sailings are occasionally cancelled in typhoon season and in rough winter weather.

half.name: Xiamen
half.blurb: A seaside city about 45 minutes away by high-speed rail includes the car-free island of Gulangyu, lined with colonial-era buildings.

half.name: Fuzhou
half.blurb: Fujian's provincial capital is about an hour away by high-speed rail and preserves the Three Lanes and Seven Alleys historic quarter.

half.name: Dehua
half.blurb: A mountain town roughly an hour and a half northwest has produced the fine white porcelain known as blanc de Chine for centuries.

full.name: Meizhou Island
full.blurb: An island shrine about two hours southeast is considered the birthplace of the sea goddess Mazu and draws pilgrims from across coastal Asia.
